title: Minimum Sum of Mountain Triplets I
statement: Call three positions `i < j < k` of the array `nums` a **mountain** when the value in the middle is strictly larger than both outer values, that is `nums[i] < nums[j]` and `nums[k] < nums[j]`. Among all mountains, find the smallest value of `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k]` and return it. If `nums` has no mountain at all, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct idea checks every triple `(i, j, k)` in O(n³), which is fine for 50 numbers. It gets simpler by enumerating only the peak `j`: once the peak is fixed, the cheapest mountain uses the smallest value to its left and the smallest value to its right. If even those smallest values are not below `nums[j]`, no mountain has its peak at `j`.

## Approach

1. Fill `rightMin` from the end so that `rightMin[j]` is the smallest value after position `j` (`Infinity` for the last position).
2. Walk the peak `j` from `1` to `n - 2`, keeping `leftMin`, the smallest value before `j`.
3. If `leftMin < nums[j]` and `rightMin[j] < nums[j]`, the triple is a mountain; keep its sum in `best` if it is smaller.
4. Fold `nums[j]` into `leftMin` before moving on.
5. Return `best`, or `-1` if it was never set.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [8, 6, 1, 5, 3]`, so `rightMin = [1, 1, 3, 3, Infinity]`.

- `j = 1` (6): `leftMin = 8` is not below 6. `leftMin` becomes 6.
- `j = 2` (1): `leftMin = 6` is not below 1. `leftMin` becomes 1.
- `j = 3` (5): `leftMin = 1 < 5` and `rightMin[3] = 3 < 5`, so `best = 1 + 5 + 3 = 9`.

The answer is `9`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one backward pass for `rightMin` and one forward pass over the peaks.
- Space: O(n) for `rightMin`.

## Pitfalls

- Both comparisons are strict: equal neighbours (like `[5, 5, 5]`) do not form a mountain.
- The peak cannot be the first or last position, so `j` runs from `1` to `n - 2`.
- Update `leftMin` only after testing `j`, so that `nums[j]` is never its own left neighbour.
- Return `-1` when no peak qualified instead of `Infinity`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rightMin[j]` | smallest value strictly after position `j` |
| `leftMin` | smallest value strictly before the current peak |
| `j` | index of the candidate peak |
| `best` | smallest mountain sum found so far |

narration.4: Start every right minimum as Infinity, which stays for the last position.
narration.5: Walk backwards so each position can reuse the minimum just after it.
narration.6: The smallest value after j is either nums[j + 1] or the smallest value after j + 1.
narration.8: Before the first possible peak, only nums[0] lies to the left.
narration.10: Try every middle position as the peak of the mountain.
narration.11: The peak works only if something on each side is strictly smaller.
narration.12: Use the smallest value on each side to get the cheapest mountain with this peak.
narration.14: Now nums[j] lies to the left of the next peak, so fold it into leftMin.
narration.16: If no peak qualified, there is no mountain and the answer is -1.
